bugs.name: Protected tag pattern validation exposes internal form field key
bugs.summary: The invalid protected-tag pattern is correctly rejected, but the visible validation alert exposes the internal key `form.NamePattern` instead of the form's user-facing “Tag Pattern” label.
bugs.expected: Reject the unmatched `[` pattern and show a user-facing validation message that identifies “Tag Pattern” and explains the invalid syntax without displaying an internal form identifier.
bugs.actual: After clicking Protect Tag, the page displayed `form.NamePattern glob pattern is invalid: unexpected end of input.` The invalid pattern was rejected, but the rendered alert exposed `form.NamePattern`.
reproSteps: Sign in as eval.
Create a fresh private personal repository named `mo-gitea-05-account-tagpattern-20260924-7f3d9b`.
Open Settings > Tags at /eval/mo-gitea-05-account-tagpattern-20260924-7f3d9b/settings/tags.
Enter the unmatched opening bracket `[` in Tag Pattern, leave Allowed users unchanged, and click Protect Tag.
Observe the validation alert above the form: `form.NamePattern glob pattern is invalid: unexpected end of input.`

bugs.name: Invalid branch-protection pattern returns 500 after saving the rule
bugs.summary: Saving an invalid branch-protection glob returns an Internal Server Error, but the rule is persisted despite the failed response.
bugs.expected: The form should reject an invalid branch-name pattern before creating a rule and show a validation error.
bugs.actual: Saving `[` displayed an HTTP 500 error page. Returning to branch settings showed a protected-branch rule named `[`. The test rule was deleted afterward.
reproSteps: Sign in to the seeded Gitea fixture and open a repository’s Settings > Branches.
Select Add New Rule and enter `[` as Protected Branch Name Pattern.
Select Save Rule and observe the Internal Server Error page.
Return to Settings > Branches and observe that the `[` rule was created.

bugs.name: Anonymous Read settings omit the site-wide mandatory sign-in override
bugs.summary: With site-wide mandatory sign-in enabled, Public Access still describes Anonymous Read as allowing logged-out access and saves it without explaining that the global login requirement overrides it.
bugs.expected: When mandatory sign-in is enabled, explain on the Public Access page that Anonymous Read does not bypass the instance-wide login requirement. Preserve the global login requirement.
bugs.actual: After saving Anonymous Read for Code, the page reports success and continues to say that users who are not logged in can access the unit with read permission, without warning that this instance requires sign-in. Signed-out visitors are correctly redirected to login under that global policy.
reproSteps: Sign in as eval, an administrator, on the seeded Gitea fixture where REQUIRE_SIGNIN_VIEW=true. Use a disposable writable public repository.
Open the repository’s Settings > Public Access. If the navigation link is absent, open /eval/<repository>/settings/public_access.
Select Anonymous Read for Code and click Update Settings. Confirm the success banner and retained selection.

Read the Anonymous Read explanation below the permissions table. It promises read access for users who are not logged in, with no qualification or warning about the enabled site-wide mandatory sign-in setting.

bugs.name: Public Access settings link is hidden until a non-default permission is saved
bugs.summary: A public repository with default unit permissions has no Public Access settings link. The page works at its known URL, and saving a non-default grant makes the missing navigation entry appear.
bugs.expected: Repository administrators should have a discoverable settings path to supported public-access permissions before a custom grant exists, including the Wiki Everyone Write option that can change access on a public repository.
bugs.actual: On a new public repository, the Settings sidebar omits Public Access. Opening the known settings/public_access URL shows a working editor with every unit set to Not Set. Saving Code Anonymous Read adds the sidebar link; restoring Not Set removes it again.
reproSteps: Sign in as eval, an administrator, and create a disposable public repository with default unit permissions. Open the new repository’s Settings page.
Inspect the Settings sidebar and observe that Public Access is absent. Do not change repository visibility or add any public-access grants first.
Open the known /<owner>/<repository>/settings/public_access URL directly as a control. Confirm the page works and every unit permission is Not Set; the sidebar link is still absent.
Select Anonymous Read for Code and click Update Settings. Confirm the saved selection and that the Public Access sidebar link now appears.
Set Code back to Not Set and click Update Settings. Confirm that all grants return to their defaults and the Public Access sidebar link disappears again.
bugs.sourceCause: The settings sidebar renders Public Access only for a private repository or an existing anonymous/everyone unit grant. A default public repository satisfies neither condition even though the editor supports meaningful permissions such as Wiki Everyone Write.

bugs.name: Template generation without Git Content breaks repository initialization
bugs.summary: Generating a template with only metadata selected creates an empty default branch. The setup commands omit the branch, and the visible New File and Upload File links lead to 404 pages.
bugs.expected: The empty generated repository should use a valid default branch such as main, show complete setup commands, and allow adding its first file through New File or Upload File.
bugs.actual: The quick guide shows `git checkout -b ` and `git push -u origin ` without a branch name. New File opens /_new// and Upload File opens /_upload//; both display 404 Not Found. A normal empty repository correctly uses main. Reproduced with Issue Labels only and Webhooks plus Branch Protection.
reproSteps: Sign in as admin and open an initialized repository with default branch main (tested with admin/bash-settings-1009).
Open Settings, enable 'Make repository a template', and save.
Return to Code and click 'Use this template'.
Enter a unique repository name, select Issue Labels only, and leave Git Content unchecked.
Create the repository and inspect its Code quick setup guide; checkout and push commands lack a branch name.
Click New File; observe a 404 at /_new//.
Return to Code and click Upload File; observe a 404 at /_upload//.

bugs.name: Duplicate branch-rule creation overwrites existing protection without confirmation
bugs.summary: Add New Rule with an existing protected-branch pattern updates the original rule using the new form defaults without warning or confirmation beforehand. This removes its saved approval requirement and administrator enforcement.
bugs.expected: Duplicate creation should reject the existing pattern or request explicit confirmation before replacing the original rule settings.
bugs.actual: A saved rule with 1 required approval and administrator enforcement enabled becomes 0 approvals with administrator enforcement disabled after the same pattern is submitted through Add New Rule with defaults. The success message reports an update and the list still contains one rule; reopening proves the submitted defaults replaced the persisted configuration.
reproSteps: Sign in to the Gitea 1.24.7 fixture and create a disposable repository initialized with a README.

Create a disposable branch and open Settings > Branches. Add a protection rule for that branch with Required approvals set to 1 and Administrators must follow branch protection rules checked. Save and reopen to confirm 1/on.
Return to Settings > Branches and choose Add New Rule. Enter exactly the same protected-branch pattern.
Leave the new form defaults: 0 required approvals and administrator enforcement unchecked. Click Save Rule.
Observe an update success message and exactly one rule in the list.
Reopen the original rule using Edit. Required approvals is 0 and administrator enforcement is unchecked. No duplicate warning or confirmation was shown before the overwrite.

matchingGuidance.rootCause: SettingsProtectedBranchPost handles RuleID 0 by loading the existing rule with the submitted RuleName, then applies all submitted values and persists that same rule. New form defaults overwrite RequiredApprovals and BlockAdminMergeOverride.

bugs.name: Existing-file editor disables direct commit despite an unprotected-file exception
bugs.summary: With branch push disabled and an existing file matched by the rule's unprotected-file pattern, the web editor disables direct commit and forces the new-branch option, despite the rule help promising that matching files can be changed directly by users with write access.
bugs.expected: For an existing file that matches an unprotected-file pattern, allow a user with write access to select Commit directly to the main branch, as the branch-rule help specifies.
bugs.actual: With main protected by Disable Push, unprotected file patterns set to `**`, protected file patterns empty, and signed commits not required, editing the existing README shows Commit directly to the main branch greyed out. The new-branch/pull-request option is forced and the button says Propose file change.
reproSteps: As the repository owner eval, create a repository initialized with a README and default branch main.

Add a protection rule for main with Disable Push selected, unprotected file patterns `**`, protected file patterns empty, Require Signed Commits unchecked, and Administrators must follow branch protection rules enabled.
Open the existing README at /eval/pushrule-repro1/_edit/main/README.md and make a change.
At Commit Changes, observe that Commit directly to the main branch is disabled, the new-branch/pull-request option is selected, and the submit button says Propose file change.

bugs.name: Renaming a protected file bypasses branch file protection
bugs.summary: With a branch rule whose protected file patterns include README.md, editing or deleting README.md directly is blocked, but renaming it in the web editor commits directly and removes README.md from the branch.
bugs.expected: Protected files cannot be changed directly, as the rule's help text says, so renaming README.md away should be rejected like an edit or delete.
bugs.actual: The rename to README-renamed.md commits directly to main. README.md then returns 404 while the rule still lists it, and renaming the file back is rejected as protected. The same bypass works through the contents API with from_path and through a git push of a pure git mv.
reproSteps: Sign in as the fixture account and create a new repository with Initialize Repository checked, so it has README.md on main.
In Settings → Branches, add a rule for main with Enable Push selected and README.md in Protected file patterns. Save it.
Edit README.md, change its content, and commit directly to main. Observe it is rejected with "path is protected and can not be changed".
Edit README.md again, change only the file name to README-renamed.md, and commit directly to main.
Observe the commit succeeds, the repository lists only README-renamed.md, and README.md returns 404 while the rule is unchanged.

bugs.name: Deleting a protected file in the web editor returns a full-page 500
bugs.summary: Deleting a file that matches a branch rule's protected file patterns replaces the page with a full-page 500 Internal Server Error instead of a form error.
bugs.expected: The delete is rejected with an in-page message that the path is protected, the same way an edit of that file is rejected, and the delete form stays available.
bugs.actual: Choosing Commit Changes on the delete page shows "500 Internal Server Error" with "DeleteRepoFile, path is protected and can not be changed [path: README.md]". The file is not deleted.
reproSteps: Sign in as the fixture account and create a new repository with Initialize Repository checked, so it has README.md on main.
In Settings → Branches, add a rule for main with Enable Push selected and README.md in Protected file patterns. Save it.
Open README.md, choose Delete File, and commit directly to main.
Observe a full-page 500 Internal Server Error reading "DeleteRepoFile, path is protected and can not be changed [path: README.md]". Reopen README.md and confirm it still exists.

bugs.name: Repository creation loses initialization and template choices after validation error
bugs.summary: When New Repository is submitted with Initialize Repository and Make repository a template ticked but another field is invalid, the re-rendered form has both boxes unticked, so correcting the error silently creates an empty, non-template repository.
bugs.expected: After a validation error, the form keeps the Initialize Repository and template choices, so correcting the invalid field creates the repository as configured.
bugs.actual: Both checkboxes come back unticked while other fields such as visibility and description are kept. Submitting after fixing only the invalid field creates an empty repository (Quick Guide, no README) that is not marked as a template. With a license or .gitignore selected, Initialize survives but the template choice is still lost.
reproSteps: Sign in as the fixture account and open New Repository.
Enter a unique name, tick Initialize Repository and Make repository a template, and enter an invalid default branch such as `bad branch`.
Choose Create Repository and observe the validation error. Both checkboxes are now unticked.
Correct only the default branch to `main` and submit.

Observe the repository is empty with the Quick Guide, and Settings shows Make repository a template unticked. As a control, the same choices with a valid branch on the first submit create a template repository with README.md.

bugs.name: Branch-rule validation discards the entire entered policy
bugs.summary: When a branch protection rule is saved with a negative required-approvals value, Gitea shows the validation error but redirects to a form that has lost every other field the user entered.
bugs.expected: The validation error keeps the entered rule (name, file patterns, push setting, checkboxes, and other values) so the user can fix only the invalid field.
bugs.actual: The page shows "Required approvals cannot be negative." but the branch name pattern, protected and unprotected file patterns, push setting, administrator enforcement, and approvals all reset to empty or defaults. Editing an existing rule this way discards the unsaved changes, and renaming one lands on a blank Add New Rule form. An invalid status-check pattern behaves the same.
reproSteps: Sign in as the fixture account and open a repository's Settings → Branches → Add New Rule.
Enter a rule name such as `release/**`, protected file patterns such as `secrets/**`, choose Enable Push, tick administrator enforcement, and set Required approvals to `-1`.
Choose Save Rule and observe "Required approvals cannot be negative."
Observe that the rule name, file patterns, push choice, administrator checkbox, and approvals have all reset.
As a control, submit the same values with Required approvals set to `2` and confirm every value is saved.

bugs.name: Documented protected-file pattern with leading slash does not protect matching files
bugs.summary: The branch-protection form's help text recommends `/docs/**/*.txt` as a protected file pattern, but patterns are matched as typed against repository paths that never start with `/`, so that pattern protects nothing.
bugs.expected: Files matching the documented example `/docs/**/*.txt`, such as docs/policy/protected.txt, cannot be created, edited, or deleted directly on the protected branch.
bugs.actual: With `/docs/**/*.txt` as the protected file pattern, creating, editing, and deleting docs/policy/protected.txt all commit directly, and the contents API and git push are not blocked either. The same rule with `docs/**/*.txt` blocks them. `/README.md` likewise protects nothing while `README.md` works.
reproSteps: Sign in as the fixture account, create a repository, and add a file docs/policy/protected.txt on main.
In Settings → Branches, add a rule for main with Enable Push and Protected file patterns set to `/docs/**/*.txt`, as in the field's help text. Save it.
Edit docs/policy/protected.txt and commit directly to main. Observe the commit succeeds.
Change the pattern to `docs/**/*.txt` and save.
Edit the file again and observe it is now rejected as protected.

bugs.name: New File editor rejects direct commits matching unprotected file patterns
bugs.summary: With branch push disabled, the web New File and Upload File flows refuse to commit directly to the branch even when the new path matches the rule's unprotected-file pattern, although the rule help says matching files can be changed directly by users with write access.
bugs.expected: A user with write access can commit a new file matching an unprotected-file pattern directly to the protected branch from New File or Upload File, as the branch-rule help specifies and as the contents API and git push already allow.
bugs.actual: With main protected by Disable Push and unprotected file patterns `**` (or `docs/**`), New File and Upload File show Commit directly to the main branch disabled with a cannot-push warning. Submitting a direct commit anyway is rejected with `Cannot commit to protected branch "main".` and the file is not created. Changing only the push mode to Enable Push lets the same file commit.
reproSteps: As the repository owner, create a repository initialized with a README and default branch main.
In Settings → Branches, add a rule for main with Disable Push, unprotected file patterns `**`, protected file patterns empty, and Require Signed Commits unchecked. Save it.
Open Add File → New File, name the file policy.txt, and enter any content.
At Commit Changes, observe Commit directly to the main branch is disabled. Submit a direct commit and observe it is rejected and policy.txt is not created.
Change only the rule's push mode to Enable Push and repeat; the file commits directly.

relatedReference.distinction: Both come from the web editor ignoring unprotected-file patterns under Disable Push, but the entry points differ: this reference covers creating a new file through New File or Upload File, and the related reference covers editing an existing file. Credit this reference for new-file or upload findings and the related one for existing-file edits.

bugs.name: Collaborators team search labels General Access teams as 'none access'
bugs.summary: In repository Settings → Collaborators, the Teams search prints each team's overall access mode as '<mode> access'. General Access teams store that mode as none and keep their real rights per unit, so a team with Code: Write is labelled 'none access'.
bugs.expected: The search result describes a General Access team's real permissions, for example as Unit Permissions like the Teams list on the same page, rather than saying it has no access.
bugs.actual: Searching the Teams box shows 'none access' under every General Access team, including one with Code: Write and other units Read, and one with every unit Read. An Administrator Access team correctly shows 'admin access'. After Add Team, the same page lists the General Access team as 'Unit Permissions' with its units. The label is display-only; adding the team grants the configured access.
reproSteps: As an organization owner, create a team with Specific repositories and General Access, set Code to Write, and keep the other units Read.
Create a repository owned by the organization and open its Settings → Collaborators.
Type the team's name into the Teams search box and wait for the result.
Observe the result says 'none access', while the team's page shows Code Write.
Select the team and click Add Team, and observe the Teams list labels it 'Unit Permissions'.

bugs.name: New Repository default branch validation error shows an internal field key
bugs.summary: Creating a repository with an invalid Default Branch name shows an error that names the field with the internal key form.DefaultBranch instead of the visible 'Default Branch' label.
bugs.expected: The validation error names the Default Branch field in readable language.
bugs.actual: On New Repository with Initialize Repository checked and bad..branch as Default Branch, Create Repository showed 'form.DefaultBranch must be a well-formed Git reference name.'
reproSteps: Open New Repository and enter a repository name.
Check Initialize Repository and enter bad..branch as the Default Branch.
Click Create Repository and read the validation error.

relatedReference.name: Protected tag pattern validation exposes internal form field key
relatedReference.distinction: Same missing-label mechanism on a different form. That entry is the protected tag pattern in branch/tag protection settings; this entry is the Default Branch field on New Repository.

bugs.name: Submitting the repository avatar form with no file shows an internal filesystem error
bugs.summary: In repository Settings, clicking Update Avatar without choosing a file shows the raw error 'Avatar.Open: open : no such file or directory' instead of asking for an image.
bugs.expected: Update Avatar with no file selected asks the user to choose an image (or is disabled), without exposing an internal error.
bugs.actual: Clicking Update Avatar with Choose new avatar left empty showed the red error 'Avatar.Open: open : no such file or directory'. Choosing a PNG afterwards uploaded normally.
reproSteps: Open a repository's Settings page.
Leave Choose new avatar empty and click Update Avatar.
Read the error shown on the page.

bugs.name: Write collaborators are offered Switch Default Branch, which opens a 404
bugs.summary: On a repository's Branches page, a collaborator with Write (not Admin) access sees the 'Switch default branch' icon next to the default branch, but it links to repository settings, which return 404 Page Not Found for non-admins.
bugs.expected: The Switch Default Branch action is shown only to users allowed to change the default branch (repository admins), or leads to a flow they can use.
bugs.actual: A Write collaborator saw the Switch Default Branch icon on Branches; clicking it opened /settings/branches, which returned HTTP 404 Page Not Found. An Admin collaborator got the default-branch form, and a Read collaborator saw no icon.
reproSteps: Add a user to a repository as a collaborator with Write access.
Sign in as that user and open the repository's Branches page.
Click the Switch default branch icon next to the default branch.

bugs.name: Branch push allowlist offers Read collaborators, then silently drops them on save
bugs.summary: In branch protection, the push allowlist offers collaborators who only have Read access. Selecting one and saving shows a success message, but the saved allowlist doesn't contain them.
bugs.expected: The push allowlist offers only users who can push, or saving explains that a selected Read collaborator needs Write access; a successful save never silently discards a visible selection.
bugs.actual: A Read collaborator appeared as a push-allowlist option. After selecting them and saving the rule, the page said 'Branch protection for rule … has been updated.', but reopening Edit showed an empty push allowlist. With the collaborator changed to Write, the same steps kept them.
reproSteps: Add a collaborator with Read access to a repository.
In Settings > Branches, add or edit a protection rule, enable the push allowlist and select that collaborator.
Save the rule, then reopen Edit and check the push allowlist.

bugs.name: Accepting a pending repository transfer returns 500 when the recipient already has a same-name repository
bugs.summary: If the recipient creates a repository with the same name while a transfer is pending, clicking Accept Transfer shows a full-page 500 Internal Server Error instead of explaining the name conflict. The API accept endpoint also returns 500.
bugs.expected: Accepting the transfer explains that the recipient already has a repository with that name (as starting a transfer into an existing name does), without a server error.
bugs.actual: After the recipient created a same-name repository, Accept Transfer returned a full-page 500 Internal Server Error; the transfer stayed pending. The API accept endpoint returned HTTP 500 as well.
reproSteps: Start a transfer of a repository to another user.
As the recipient, create a repository with the same name.
As the recipient, open the transferred repository and click Accept Transfer.

bugs.name: Project board shows New Issue, Labels and Milestones links that 404 for users without Issues access
bugs.summary: When a user can read a repository's Projects but not its Issues, the project board still shows New Issue, Labels and Milestones buttons, and each opens a 404 page. The repository header correctly hides Issues for that user.
bugs.expected: The project board only shows New Issue, Labels and Milestones to users who can access the Issues unit.
bugs.actual: On a private repository with Projects set to Everyone Read and Issues not shared, a non-member viewing the project board saw New Issue, Labels and Milestones; clicking New Issue opened a 404 Not Found page, as did the other two.
reproSteps: In a private repository, create a project and set Public Access so Projects is readable by everyone while Issues is not.
As a non-member, open the repository's project board.
Click New Issue (and Labels, Milestones) above the board.

relatedReference.distinction: Both show a control that leads to a 404 for users without access. That entry is the Branches page Switch Default Branch for Write collaborators; this entry is the project board's issue links for users without Issues access.

bugs.name: Repositories generated from a template don't show the detected license
bugs.summary: A repository generated from a template with Git Content has the template's LICENSE file byte for byte, but its sidebar has no license link and the license API returns none, while the template, forks and normally created repositories show it.
bugs.expected: A generated repository whose LICENSE matches a recognized license shows that license in the sidebar and API, as the source template does.
bugs.actual: An MIT template showed Readme, MIT and size in the sidebar. A repository generated from it with Git Content had an identical LICENSE but showed only Readme and size, and the license API returned []. It stayed missing across reloads; one ordinary commit to the generated repository made MIT appear.
reproSteps: Create a repository initialized with the MIT license and mark it as a template.
Use this template to generate a new repository with Git Content.
Compare the sidebar of the template and the generated repository.

bugs.name: Invalid repository name in Settings discards the other unsaved basic-settings edits
bugs.summary: In repository Settings > Basic Settings, submitting an invalid repository name shows the right validation error but redraws the form from the saved values, so the other edits made in the same submission (description, website, template checkbox) are lost.
bugs.expected: The invalid name is rejected with feedback while the other entered values stay in the form, so the owner can fix the name and save without re-entering them.
bugs.actual: With the name set to 'bad name !', the description to 'Recovery draft 1024' and the website to 'https://example.com', Update Settings showed the name validation error, but the description and website reverted to their previous empty values and the name reverted too.
reproSteps: Open a repository's Settings.
Enter an invalid name such as 'bad name !' and also change the description and website.
Click Update Settings and check the form fields after the error.

bugs.name: Whitespace-only tag protection pattern saves as an empty rule, and editing a rule to whitespace disables it
bugs.summary: In Settings > Tags, an empty Tag Pattern is rejected, but a pattern of only spaces or tabs is accepted with a success message and saved as an empty pattern that protects no tag. Editing an existing working rule to whitespace likewise reports success and silently removes its protection.
bugs.expected: A whitespace-only Tag Pattern is rejected like an empty one, on both create and edit, and an existing protection rule is never blanked.
bugs.actual: Three spaces (or ' \t  ') were accepted with 'The repository settings have been updated.' and saved as a blank-looking rule; reopening Edit showed an empty pattern. Editing a working 'v*' rule to three spaces reported success, blanked the pattern, and the owner could then create a tag that the rule had blocked moments earlier.
reproSteps: In a repository's Settings > Tags, add a protection rule with pattern v* and confirm creating a tag v1-test is refused.
Edit that rule, replace the pattern with three spaces and save.
Check the saved rule and try creating a tag matching v* again.

relatedReference.name: Protected tag pattern validation exposes internal form field key
relatedReference.distinction: Same Tag Pattern field. That entry is an invalid pattern's error naming form.NamePattern; this entry is a whitespace-only pattern being accepted and saved as empty.

bugs.name: Administrator-team members can add and remove repository teams when the organization restricts it to owners
bugs.summary: With the organization setting 'Repository admin can add and remove access for teams' turned off, a non-owner who gets repository admin through an Administrator-access team still sees the team controls under Settings > Collaborators and can add or remove teams, including their own.
bugs.expected: When the organization turns off repository admins' ability to change team access, only organization owners can add or remove teams on its repositories; a repository admin who isn't an owner is told the change is restricted to organization owners.
bugs.actual: A member of the repository's Administrator Access team, who is not an organization owner, still saw an active Remove control for the team. Remove > Yes deleted the team association, and the user immediately lost access to the private repository (404). A directly added admin collaborator is correctly blocked.
reproSteps: As an organization owner, create a private repository in the organization and a team with Administrator Access to it.
Add a non-owner user to that team.
In the organization's settings, uncheck 'Repository admin can add and remove access for teams' and save.
As the non-owner team member, open the repository's Settings > Collaborators.
Remove the team (or add another team) and check whether the change is blocked.

bugs.name: Rejecting a private repository transfer leaves the recipient able to read the repository
bugs.summary: Transferring a private repository to a user with no access to it quietly adds that user as a Read collaborator so they can review the transfer. When the recipient rejects the transfer, that access is never removed, so they can keep reading the private repository's code after the transfer is gone.
bugs.expected: After a private repository transfer is rejected, a recipient who had no access before the transfer can no longer see the repository.
bugs.actual: After maya rejected the transfer of alex's private repository ('Repository transfer was rejected.'), the Accept/Reject controls disappeared, but after refresh maya could still open the repository and read its full README. maya had not been a collaborator before the transfer.
reproSteps: As one user, create a private repository with a README and no collaborators; confirm a second user gets 404 on it.
In Settings > Danger Zone, transfer the repository to the second user.
As the second user, open the repository and click Reject Transfer.
Refresh and check whether the second user can still open the repository and read its files.

bugs.name: A user not allowed by a protected-tag rule can still delete a protected tag
bugs.summary: With a protected-tag rule (for example release-*) that allows only certain users, a Write collaborator who isn't allowed is correctly blocked from creating a matching tag but can still delete an existing one from the Tags page or the API. The delete check uses the tag's original publisher instead of the person deleting it, so deleting a tag published by an allowed user always passes.
bugs.expected: Deleting a tag that matches a protected-tag rule is refused for users the rule doesn't allow, and the tag stays listed.
bugs.actual: With a release-* rule allowing only eval, Write collaborator alex was refused when creating a release-* tag ('The tag name is protected.') but clicking Delete Tag > Yes on eval's release-1 showed 'The tag has been deleted.' and '0 Tags'.
reproSteps: As the owner, create a tag release-1 and add a protected-tag rule release-* allowing only yourself; add a second user as a Write collaborator.
As the second user, try to create a tag release-2 and confirm it is refused as protected.
As the second user, open the Tags page and delete release-1.
Check whether the deletion is refused and release-1 is still listed.

bugs.name: Rejected collaborator role change shows the new role with no error
bugs.summary: On Settings > Collaborators, if a role change is rejected by the server (for example an administrator who lowered their own role to Read then picks Administrator again without refreshing), the role menu still switches to the chosen role and no error appears. The menu updates whatever the server responds; permissions themselves are enforced correctly.
bugs.expected: When a collaborator role change fails, the page says so and the role menu keeps showing the role that is actually saved.
bugs.actual: After alex lowered his own role from Administrator to Read, choosing Administrator again from the same menu showed 'Administrator' with no toast or error, while the change request returned 404. Refreshing showed 404 Not Found, and the owner still saw alex as Read.
reproSteps: As the owner, add a second user as an Administrator collaborator on a private repository.
As the second user, open Settings > Collaborators and change your own role to Read.
Without refreshing, choose Administrator from the same role menu.
Check whether an error is shown and what role the menu displays; then refresh.

bugs.name: Publishing a draft release whose tag is protected shows a full-page 500
bugs.summary: When a draft release uses a tag name that a protected-tag rule doesn't allow the user to create, clicking Publish Release from the Edit Release page replaces the form with a full-page 500 Internal Server Error, and the unsaved title and notes are lost. Creating the same release from New Release shows a readable error instead.
bugs.expected: Publishing is rejected with a readable protected-tag error in the form, as on New Release, and the draft stays editable.
bugs.actual: Publish Release returned a full-page 500 Internal Server Error ("UpdateRelease, release tag name is protected"); the draft wasn't published and the unsaved edits were lost.
reproSteps: In a repository's Settings > Tags, protect a tag pattern so that you aren't allowed to create matching tags.
Create a draft release with a new tag name matching that pattern and save it as a draft.
Edit the draft and click Publish Release.
Check whether a readable error or a 500 page appears.

bugs.name: Archived repository still opens the wiki editor, and Save Page ends in a 404
bugs.summary: In an archived repository, the wiki hides its create and edit buttons, but opening the wiki's New Page (or Edit) URL directly still shows an editable form with Save Page. Saving replaces the page with a full 404 instead of saying the repository is archived and read-only.
bugs.expected: Wiki create and edit URLs in an archived repository refuse up front with a read-only message, as other editors in archived repositories do.
bugs.actual: The wiki New Page URL showed the title, content and Save Page controls despite the Archived badge; clicking Save Page showed a full-page 404 Not Found. Nothing was saved.
reproSteps: In a repository with the wiki enabled, create a wiki page and note the New Page URL (ending /wiki?action=_new).
Archive the repository in Settings.
Open the wiki's New Page URL directly, enter a title and content, and click Save Page.
Check what the page shows.

bugs.name: Whitespace-only branch protection pattern saves a blank rule
bugs.summary: In a repository's branch protection settings, a rule's Protected Branch Name Pattern made only of spaces is accepted with a success message and saved as a blank-looking rule. An empty pattern is rejected, but spaces aren't trimmed.
bugs.expected: A branch protection pattern made only of whitespace is rejected like an empty one.
bugs.actual: Editing a rule's pattern to three spaces saved with a success message; the branch protection list showed a blank rule name, and reopening it showed a blank-looking pattern.
reproSteps: In a repository's Settings > Branches, add a protection rule with a normal pattern and save.
Edit the rule, replace the pattern with only spaces, and save.
Reload the branch protection list and reopen the rule.

relatedReference.name: Whitespace-only tag protection pattern saves as an empty rule, and editing a rule to whitespace disables it
relatedReference.distinction: Same missing whitespace check, but that entry is tag protection; this entry is branch protection.

bugs.name: Archived issue detail offers New Issue button that opens a 404
bugs.summary: After archiving a private repository, an existing issue still offers New Issue. Clicking it opens 404 Not Found rather than an available action or an archive explanation.
bugs.expected: An archived repository should not offer an unusable New Issue action; hide or disable it consistently with the archived issues list, or explain why creation is unavailable.
bugs.actual: Existing issue detail shows New Issue, and clicking it loads /issues/new with 404 Not Found. The existing issue otherwise correctly reports that comments are unavailable because the repository is archived.
reproSteps: Create a disposable initialized repository and an issue.
Archive the repository through Settings and confirm.
Reopen the existing issue and click its visible New Issue button.
Observe that /issues/new displays 404 Not Found.

relatedReference.distinction: The existing reference covers an archived wiki editor offering Save Page and then returning 404. This entry covers the visible New Issue button on an existing archived issue leading to a 404.

matchingGuidance.scope: Grade the unusable New Issue action offered on an archived issue detail page, not the intended restriction against creating issues in archived repositories.

reviewEvidence.basis: Explicit user acceptance as a related severity-3 entry based on two Mo reports. Independent verdicts pending at approval.
reviewEvidence.severityReason: An offered action navigates to a 404 rather than an available form or archive explanation.
analysis: Two Mo submissions report the same archive lifecycle and visible New Issue action ending in 404.
The issue creation restriction itself is expected; the user approved the unusable offered action as the defect.
limitations: No independent browser verdict or complete source-cause review available at approval.

bugs.name: Submitting a stale issue form after the repository is archived shows a raw JSON error
bugs.summary: If a repository is archived while a New Issue (or comment) form is open, submitting the form shows a red "Network error SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'N', \"Not found.\" is not valid JSON" instead of saying the repository is archived and read-only.
bugs.expected: Submitting a form in a repository that has since been archived shows a clear message that the repository is archived and read-only.
bugs.actual: Clicking Create Issue showed the red network SyntaxError banner about "Not found." not being valid JSON; the form kept its input and nothing mentioned the archive.
reproSteps: Open a repository's New Issue form and fill it in.
In another tab, archive the repository.
Back in the first tab, click Create Issue and read the message.

bugs.name: An allowed user can't delete a protected tag created by someone outside the rule
bugs.summary: Deleting a tag that matches a protected-tag rule checks whether the tag's creator is allowed by the rule, not the person deleting it. So a collaborator on the rule's allowlist is refused ("The tag name is protected.") when deleting a matching tag created by a user who isn't on it.
bugs.expected: A user allowed by a protected-tag rule can delete any tag matching that rule, whoever created the tag.
bugs.actual: As an allowed Write collaborator, deleting matching tags created by the repository owner (not on the allowlist) showed "The tag name is protected." and the tags stayed; deleting a matching tag the collaborator created themselves worked.
reproSteps: Add a protected-tag rule (for example test-*) that allows a collaborator but not the repository owner.
As the owner, create a tag matching the rule.
As the allowed collaborator, try to delete that tag from the Tags page.
Check the message and whether the tag was deleted.

relatedReference.name: A user not allowed by a protected-tag rule can still delete a protected tag
relatedReference.distinction: Same check against the tag's creator instead of the deleter, but that entry is a disallowed user deleting an allowed creator's tag; this entry is an allowed user being blocked from deleting a disallowed creator's tag.

bugs.name: Adding the repository's owner as a collaborator does nothing and shows no message
bugs.summary: On a repository's Collaborators settings, entering the repository's own owner (the user who owns a personal repository, or the organization that owns an organization repository) and clicking Add Collaborator just reloads the page with no error. Gitea already has the message "Cannot add an owner as a collaborator." and shows it when an organization's owner is added, but not for the repository's own owner.
bugs.expected: Adding the repository's own owner shows an explicit error such as "Cannot add an owner as a collaborator.", like Gitea's other rejected additions.
bugs.actual: Entering the owner's name and clicking Add Collaborator reloaded the page with no success or error message and no change to the list. A nonexistent user, a duplicate collaborator and an organization owner each showed an error message.
reproSteps: Open the Collaborators settings of a repository owned by your user account.
Enter your own username (the repository owner) and click Add Collaborator.
Check whether any message appears.

bugs.name: Changing a Read collaborator to Write on a public repository shows the new role but access stays Read
bugs.summary: On a public user-owned repository, changing a collaborator from Read to Write or Administrator in Settings > Collaborators shows the new role, even after a reload, but the collaborator's actual permission stays read. The same change on a private repository, or from Write to Administrator, works.
bugs.expected: Choosing Write or Administrator for a Read collaborator gives them that access, as the permission API and branch protection lists reflect.
bugs.actual: After changing the collaborator from Read to Write (and to Administrator), the Collaborators page showed the new role, but the collaborator permission endpoint still returned permission "read".
reproSteps: On a public repository you own, add a collaborator with Read permission.
In Settings > Collaborators, change their permission to Write, and reload.
Check the collaborator's effective permission, for example with GET /api/v1/repos/<owner>/<repo>/collaborators/<user>/permission.

bugs.name: Branch protection saves an invalid protected-file pattern, which silently disables file protection
bugs.summary: A branch protection rule's Protected file patterns field accepts an invalid glob such as '[' and reports success. The pattern is stored as entered, but when it's used the invalid pattern is skipped, so the protected files are no longer protected, with no warning to the repository owner. Tag protection rejects the same invalid pattern when it's saved.
bugs.expected: Saving a branch protection rule with an invalid protected-file pattern is rejected with an error, as tag protection does, instead of saving a pattern that protects nothing.
bugs.actual: Changing Protected file patterns from README.md to '[' saved with a success message and the rule reopened showing '['; a writer's direct edit of README.md, which had been blocked, then succeeded.
reproSteps: Add a branch protection rule with Protected file patterns set to a file such as README.md, and confirm a writer's direct edit of that file is blocked.
Edit the rule, change the pattern to '[' and save.
As the writer, edit and commit that file directly to the branch.

bugs.name: Confirming a stale merge after the repository is archived shows a raw JSON error
bugs.summary: If a repository is archived while a pull request page is open, confirming the merge from that page shows a red "Network error SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'N', \"Not found.\" is not valid JSON" instead of saying the repository is archived and read-only.
bugs.expected: Confirming a merge in a repository that has since been archived shows a clear message that the repository is archived and read-only.
bugs.actual: Clicking the merge button and confirming showed the red network SyntaxError banner about "Not found." not being valid JSON. The merge form stayed open and nothing mentioned the archive. Merging the same way without archiving succeeds, and reloading the archived pull request hides the merge box.
reproSteps: Open a mergeable pull request in a repository you can merge in.
In another tab, archive the repository.
Back in the first tab, choose a merge style, confirm the merge and read the message.
bugs.sourceCause: routers/web/web.go runs context.RepoMustNotBeArchived() before MergePullRequest on POST /pulls/{index}/merge; it answers with a plain-text 404 "Not found.", which web_src/js/features/common-fetch-action.ts parses as JSON and reports as a network SyntaxError.

relatedReference.distinction: Same archived-repository guard and JSON parse error, but on a different form. That entry is the New Issue or comment form; this entry is the pull request merge confirmation.

bugs.name: Submitting a stale pull request form after the repository is archived shows a raw JSON error
bugs.summary: If a repository is archived while a compare page's New Pull Request form is open, clicking Create Pull Request shows a red "Network error SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'N', \"Not found.\" is not valid JSON" instead of saying the repository is archived and read-only.
bugs.expected: Submitting a new pull request in a repository that has since been archived shows a clear message that the repository is archived and read-only.
bugs.actual: Clicking Create Pull Request showed the red network SyntaxError banner about "Not found." not being valid JSON; the form kept its title and description and nothing mentioned the archive. The same form creates the pull request when the repository isn't archived, and reloading the compare page after archiving hides New Pull Request.
reproSteps: Push a branch with a change and open its compare page, then click New Pull Request and fill in the form.
In another tab, archive the repository.
Back in the first tab, click Create Pull Request and read the message.
bugs.sourceCause: routers/web/web.go runs context.RepoMustNotBeArchived() before CompareAndPullRequestPost on POST /compare/*; it answers with a plain-text 404 "Not found.", which web_src/js/features/common-fetch-action.ts parses as JSON and reports as a network SyntaxError.

relatedReference.distinction: Same archived-repository guard and JSON parse error, but on a different form. That entry is the New Issue or comment form; this entry is the Create Pull Request form on the compare page.

bugs.name: Direct Write collaborator loses write access on public organization repositories after leaving their last team
bugs.summary: When a user who is also a direct Write collaborator on an organization's public repository is removed from their last team in that organization, they stop being an organization member and lose write access to the repository. The Collaborators page still lists them as Write, and changing their role there doesn't restore access.
bugs.expected: A direct collaborator grant keeps applying after the user leaves the organization's teams, as it does for private repositories and for collaborators who were never organization members.
bugs.actual: alex had team Write and a direct Write collaborator grant on a public and a private organization repository. After removing alex from the team, the public repository's Collaborators page still listed alex as Write, but alex had no New Release button, release creation returned 403 and editing a file returned 404. The private repository kept Write. Leaving alex in a second team of the organization kept Write on both repositories.
reproSteps: In an organization, create a public repository and a team with Write access to it.
Add a user to that team, and also add the same user as a Write collaborator under the repository's Settings > Collaborators.
Remove the user from the team, so they are no longer in any team of the organization.
As the owner, see that the Collaborators page still lists the user as Write.
As the user, open the repository's Releases page or try to edit a file and see that write actions are gone.
bugs.sourceCause: services/org/team.go removeTeamMember recalculates access (keeping the collaborator grant), then removeInvalidOrgUser calls RemoveOrgUser when no teams remain. services/org/user.go RemoveOrgUser deletes the user's Access rows for every public organization repository without recalculating them from their Collaboration rows, so models/perm/access accessLevel falls back to public Read. Changing the collaborator role only updates an existing Access row, so it can't recreate the deleted one.

matchingGuidance.scope: Reports that a direct collaborator loses write access after being removed from an organization team, removed from the organization, or leaving it, while the Collaborators page still shows their role, match this entry.

relatedReference.distinction: Both show a collaborator role the user's effective access doesn't match on a public repository. That entry is upgrading a Read collaborator to Write on a user-owned repository; this entry is a Write collaborator losing access when they leave an organization's last team.

bugs.name: Opening an empty repository with Code and Issues disabled redirects to a 404 Pull Requests page
bugs.summary: For a repository with no commits whose Code and Issues units are disabled, every link to the repository (its name in lists, the header and search) redirects to /pulls, which shows 404 Not Found. Pull Requests and Releases don't work in an empty repository, while the enabled Wiki, Projects and Packages sections open normally.
bugs.expected: Opening the repository lands on a section that works, such as Wiki or Projects, or explains why there is nothing to show.
bugs.actual: Clicking the repository in the owner's repository list went to /<owner>/<repo>/pulls and showed '404 Not Found. The page you are trying to reach either does not exist or you are not authorized to view it.' The tab bar on that page listed only Packages, Projects, Wiki and Settings, and /wiki, /projects and /packages each opened normally. With Pull Requests also disabled, the redirect went to /releases, also a 404. The same settings on a repository with commits open /pulls normally, and disabling only Code opens /issues.
reproSteps: Create a repository without initializing it, so it has no commits.
In its Settings, turn off Code and Issues and save, leaving Wiki, Projects and Packages enabled.
Open the repository from a repository list or its name in the header.
Observe the redirect to /pulls and the 404 Not Found page.
bugs.sourceCause: routers/web/repo/view.go checkHomeCodeViewable redirects to the highest-priority readable unit when Code isn't readable, without checking whether that unit's pages work in an empty repository. The Pull Requests and Releases routes are gated by repo.MustBeNotEmpty, which returns 404 for empty repositories.

matchingGuidance.scope: Reports that opening an empty repository with Code disabled redirects to a 404 Pull Requests or Releases page match this entry.

relatedReference.distinction: Both are in-product navigation that ends on a 404. That entry is the Branches page Switch default branch icon for Write collaborators; this entry is the repository home redirect for an empty repository with Code and Issues disabled.

bugs.name: Commenting from a stale issue page after the repository is archived shows a raw JSON error
bugs.summary: If a repository is archived while an existing issue's page is open, submitting a comment from that page shows a red "Network error SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'N', \"Not found.\" is not valid JSON" instead of saying the repository is archived and read-only.
bugs.expected: Commenting on an issue in a repository that has since been archived shows a clear message that the repository is archived and read-only.
bugs.actual: Clicking Comment showed the red network SyntaxError banner about "Not found." not being valid JSON, and the draft stayed in the editor. Commenting before archiving works, and reloading the archived issue shows 'This repo is archived. You cannot comment on issues.'
reproSteps: Open an existing issue and type a comment.
In another tab, archive the repository.
Back in the first tab, click Comment and read the message.
bugs.sourceCause: The issue comment route (routers/web/web.go, POST /issues/{index}/comments) rejects archived repositories with a plain-text 404 "Not found.", which web_src/js/features/common-fetch-action.ts parses as JSON and reports as a network SyntaxError.

relatedReference.distinction: Same archived-repository guard and JSON parse error. That entry's reproduction is the New Issue form; this entry is the Comment form on an existing issue.
